newsitem.title: BRAZIL: CVRD shrs seen steady after privatization.
newsitem.headline: CVRD shrs seen steady after privatization.

text.p: Investors should not expect a surge in the stock price of Brazilian state mining conglomerate Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) after the government sells a 45 percent controlling stake on Tuesday, analysts said.

The analysts predicted Vale's shares will remain steady in the short-term and some said they may even be hit by profit-taking as the company's stock has already reached a price reflecting the firm's post-privatization prospects.
"Positive expectations on Vale's sale have already been priced in. The company's stock prices are already fair enough," said Adriana Lacombe, mining analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Brazil.

Vale's voting stock has fallen 10.25 percent on the Sao Paulo bolsa since the government early last month announced a 26.67 reais per share base price for the April 29 auction of a controlling stake. The stock traded at 28.90 reais this morning. The government will be selling voting, or common stock.
The company's preferred shares, which do not have voting rights and are the most liquid, have slipped 0.37 percent to 27 reais in the same period.

Analysts said the prices of Vale voting and non-voting shares fell to bring them more in line with the government's announced minimum price, which was based on average market values over the preceeding six months.
CVRD common stock last Friday traded 8.36 percent over the minimum price, reflecting expectations that the controlling stake in CVRD will be sold at a premium.

Although analysts have no doubt that CVRD will become more efficient and competitive in private hands, they said it will take some time for investors to figure out to what extent the company will benefit from new management.

"It is difficult to predict how much CVRD will gain from its privatization," said Isabela Lacombe, analyst at Rio-based investment bank Banco Icatu, referring to the company's post-privatization outlook.

Analysts said CVRD's prospects also depend on who wins the auction. Two groups, one led by local industrial conglomerate Grupo Votorantim and South Africa's Anglo American and another headed by private steelmaker CSN, have qualified to bid.
Some analysts think CVRD would be better off with the Votorantim consortium, named Valecom, because it includes major global mining companies.

In addition to Anglo-American, the Valecom group includes Brazilian metal and metallurgical group Caemi, 40 percent owned by Japan's Mitsui & Co Ltd. Eleven other Japanese steel firms are backing the consortium.
"The Valecom group has members that have more to do with CVRD's core business," said Alvaro Maia, head of equity sales for Caspian Securities in Brazil.
Forty-five percent of the voting shares of CVRD, the world's largest iron ore exporter, will be auctioned Tuesday unless the sale is delayed by court cases.
The privatization has been hit by a slew of legal roadblocks.
The Supreme Federal Tribunal in Brasilia, the country's highest court, rejected one claim that the sale is inconstitutional and will rule on another later today.
Four regional courts have also issued injunctions suspending the sale. The BNDES National Development Bank said its lawyers had already lodged appeals against the injunctions.
The privatization also faces over 100 other applications for injunctions around the country.
